1:1|How she sits alone,
the city once full of people!
She has become like a widow,
once great among the nations.
A princess among the provinces
has been put to forced labor.|Keeps the opening lament, female personification, and reversal from princess to forced labor.

1:2|She weeps and weeps in the night,
tears running down her cheeks.
Among all her lovers
there is no one to comfort her.
All her friends have betrayed her;
they have become her enemies.|Retains doubled weeping, lovers/friends, and the comfort refrain.

1:3|Judah has gone into exile through affliction
and harsh servitude.
She lives among the nations
but finds no resting place.
All her pursuers overtake her
in the narrow places.|Keeps the ambiguous relation of affliction to exile and the trapped-space image.

1:4|The roads to Zion mourn,
for no one comes to the appointed feast.
All her gates are desolate;
her priests groan.
Her virgins grieve,
and she herself is bitter.|Preserves personified roads, religious gathering, and specific virgin term.

1:5|Her foes have become her masters;
her enemies are at ease.
The **LORD** has made her suffer
for her many rebellions.
Her little children have gone captive
before the enemy.|Keeps explicit divine agency and children's captivity without adding a moral rationale beyond the text.

1:6|All her splendor has departed
from daughter Zion.
Her officials have become like deer
that find no pasture.
Without strength they walk
before the pursuer.|Follows the read from-daughter form and retains exhausted deer imagery.

1:7|In her days of affliction and wandering,
Jerusalem remembers all her treasures from long ago.
When her people fell into the enemy's hand,
there was no one to help her.
Her enemies saw her
and laughed at her downfall.|Preserves memory of former treasures and the enemy's derision.

1:8|Jerusalem has sinned grievously;
so she has become unclean.
All who honored her now despise her,
for they have seen her nakedness.
She too groans
and turns away.|Keeps impurity and exposed nakedness as the poem's imagery, with a note distinguishing it from an endorsement of humiliation.

1:10|The enemy stretched out his hand
over all her treasures.
She saw nations enter her sanctuary,
those you commanded
not to enter your assembly.|Retains the shift to addressing God and the sanctuary's violation.

1:11|All her people groan, searching for bread.
They trade their treasures for food
to keep themselves alive.
“Look, **LORD**, and see:
I have become despised.|Follows the read treasures form and marks the city's renewed speech.

1:12|Does this mean nothing to you, all who pass by?
Look and see whether any pain is like my pain,
like what has been done to me,
what the **LORD** inflicted
on the day of his burning anger.|Uses the rhetorical-question reading of the difficult opening and retains divine affliction.

1:13|From on high he sent fire into my bones,
and it mastered them.
He spread a net for my feet
and turned me back.
He left me desolate,
sick all day long.|Keeps fire, bones, net, and the repeated divine actions rather than flattening them into distress.

1:14|The yoke of my rebellions was bound by his hand;
woven together, they rose onto my neck.
He made my strength fail.
The Lord handed me over
to those I cannot withstand.|Preserves the difficult bound-yoke reading and the Lord distinct from **LORD**.

1:15|The Lord has cast aside
all the mighty men within me.
He called an assembly against me
to crush my young men.
The Lord has trodden virgin daughter Judah
as grapes in a winepress.|Keeps the appointed-assembly reversal and bodily winepress violence.

1:16|For these things I weep;
my eye, my eye pours out water.
Far from me is a comforter,
one who could restore my life.
My children are desolate,
for the enemy has prevailed.”|Retains the repeated eye and lack of life-restoring comfort.

1:17|Zion spreads out her hands;
no one comforts her.
The **LORD** has commanded
that Jacob's neighbors become his foes.
Jerusalem has become unclean among them.|Marks the narrative interruption and preserves commanded hostility.

1:18|“The **LORD** is righteous,
for I rebelled against his command.
Listen, all you peoples,
and see my pain.
My virgins and young men
have gone into captivity.|Keeps confession and appeal together without allowing one to cancel the other.

1:19|I called to my lovers,
but they deceived me.
My priests and elders died in the city
as they searched for food
to keep themselves alive.|Preserves failed allies and leaders dying in their search for sustenance.

1:21|They hear my groaning,
but no one comforts me.
All my enemies hear of my disaster;
they rejoice that you have done it.
Bring the day you announced,
and let them become like me.|Uses a petition reading for the announced day and preserves the request for others to share her fate.

1:22|Let all their evil come before you.
Deal with them as you dealt with me
for all my rebellions.
My groans are many,
and my heart is sick.”|Retains retribution petition and exhausted closing without a consoling addition.

2:1|How the Lord has covered daughter Zion
with the cloud of his anger!
He hurled Israel's splendor
from heaven to earth.
On the day of his anger
he did not remember his footstool.|Preserves cloud, downward casting, and footstool imagery.

2:2|The Lord swallowed up without pity
all Jacob's dwellings.
In his fury he tore down
daughter Judah's fortresses.
He brought them to the ground,
profaning the kingdom and its rulers.|Keeps swallowing and lack of pity with royal profanation.

2:3|In burning anger he cut off
every horn of Israel.
He drew back his right hand
in the face of the enemy.
He burned in Jacob like a flaming fire,
devouring all around.|Retains horn and withdrawn hand as bodily images of lost strength and protection.

2:4|He drew his bow like an enemy,
his right hand poised like a foe.
He killed all that delighted the eye.
In daughter Zion's tent
he poured out his wrath like fire.|Keeps God like an enemy and the full agency of killing.

2:5|The Lord has become like an enemy.
He swallowed up Israel,
swallowed all her palaces,
destroyed her fortresses.
He multiplied mourning and moaning
in daughter Judah.|Retains repeated swallowing and paired sounds of grief.

2:7|The Lord rejected his altar,
repudiated his sanctuary.
He handed the walls of her palaces
over to the enemy.
They raised their voices in the **LORD**'s house
as on a feast day.|Keeps Lord/**LORD** distinction and the bitter festival comparison.

2:8|The **LORD** planned to destroy
daughter Zion's wall.
He stretched out a measuring line
and did not draw back his destroying hand.
He made rampart and wall mourn;
together they languished.|Preserves deliberate measured destruction and personified fortifications.

2:10|Daughter Zion's elders sit on the ground in silence.
They throw dust on their heads
and put on sackcloth.
Jerusalem's virgins
bow their heads to the ground.|Preserves age/gender groups and bodily mourning gestures.

2:11|My eyes are spent with tears;
my insides churn.
My liver is poured out on the ground
because my people are shattered,
because children and nursing infants faint
in the town's squares.|Retains liver as an ancient bodily image and children's collapse.

2:12|They ask their mothers,
“Where are grain and wine?”
They faint like the wounded
in the city squares,
their lives pouring away
in their mothers' arms.|Keeps the children's question and the outpouring of life without euphemism.

2:13|What can I say for you? To what can I compare you,
daughter Jerusalem?
What can I set beside you to comfort you,
virgin daughter Zion?
Your breach is as vast as the sea.
Who can heal you?|Preserves the search for comparison and the unanswered question.

2:14|Your prophets saw empty and hollow visions for you.
They did not expose your guilt
to restore your fortunes.
They saw for you empty oracles
that led you astray.|Follows the read fortunes form and retains prophetic failure without adding a sermon.

2:15|All who pass by clap their hands at you;
they hiss and shake their heads
at daughter Jerusalem:
“Is this the city they called
perfect in beauty,
the joy of the whole earth?”|Keeps mocking gestures and the city's former titles in the taunt.

2:16|All your enemies open their mouths against you;
they hiss and grind their teeth.
They say, “We have swallowed her!
This is the day we waited for.
We have reached it; we have seen it!”|Preserves enemy triumph and the doubled arrival/seeing claim.

2:17|The **LORD** has done what he planned,
fulfilled the word he commanded long ago.
He tore down without pity;
he let the enemy rejoice over you
and raised the horn of your foes.|Retains fulfilled intention and the enemy's raised horn against Israel's cut horns.

2:18|Their hearts cry out to the Lord.
Wall of daughter Zion,
let tears flow like a torrent day and night.
Give yourself no rest;
let the pupil of your eye never cease.|Keeps the abrupt address to the wall and literal eye image, explained in a note.

2:19|Rise, cry out in the night,
at the beginning of each watch.
Pour out your heart like water
before the Lord.
Lift your hands to him for your children's lives;
they faint from hunger at every street corner.|Preserves night watches, water image, and petition for starving children.

2:20|“Look, **LORD**, and see:
whom have you treated this way?
Should women eat their own offspring,
the children they have nurtured?
Should priest and prophet be killed
in the Lord's sanctuary?|Keeps direct protest, cannibalism, and both divine designations without sensational detail.

2:21|Young and old lie on the ground in the streets.
My virgins and young men have fallen by the sword.
You killed them on the day of your anger;
you slaughtered without pity.|Retains the direct accusation and repeated killing verbs.

2:22|You summoned my terrors from every side
as though to a feast day.
On the day of the **LORD**'s anger
there was no fugitive or survivor.
Those I nurtured and raised,
my enemy consumed.”|Preserves the inverted feast and maternal closing grief.
3:1|I am the man who has seen affliction\nunder the rod of his fury.|Keeps the male speaker and unnamed he at the opening.
3:2|He led me and made me walk\nin darkness, without light.|Preserves divine compulsion and negative contrast.
3:3|Against me he turns his hand\nagain and again, all day long.|Keeps the repeated hostile action and duration.
3:4|He wore away my flesh and skin;\nhe broke my bones.|Retains concrete bodily damage.
3:5|He built siegeworks against me,\nsurrounding me with bitterness and hardship.|Unpacks the building-against image while keeping bitter encirclement.
3:6|He made me live in dark places,\nlike those long dead.|Preserves the burial-like dwelling comparison.
3:7|He walled me in so I cannot escape;\nhe made my bronze chain heavy.|Keeps confinement and the stated material of the bond.
3:8|Even when I cry out and plead,\nhe shuts out my prayer.|Retains blocked prayer without an immediate reassurance.
3:9|He blocked my roads with cut stone\nand twisted my paths.|Keeps both obstruction and distortion.
3:10|He is a bear lying in wait for me,\na lion in hiding.|Preserves God as predator and follows the read lion form.
3:11|He forced me off my paths and tore me apart;\nhe left me desolate.|Keeps the violent tearing and resulting isolation.
3:12|He drew his bow\nand set me up as a target for his arrow.|Retains the target image and deliberate positioning.
3:13|He drove the sons of his quiver\ninto my kidneys.|Preserves both ancient arrow metaphor and bodily organ, explained in vocabulary.
3:14|I became a laughingstock to all my people,\nthe subject of their songs all day long.|Keeps my people rather than silently emending to all peoples.
3:15|He filled me with bitter things\nand made me drink my fill of wormwood.|Retains bitter eating/drinking and named plant.
3:16|He ground my teeth with gravel\nand pressed me into ashes.|Keeps concrete humiliation without reducing it to sadness.
3:17|You have driven my life away from peace;\nI have forgotten what good is.|Preserves the sudden second-person turn and loss of remembered good.
3:18|I said, “My endurance is gone,\nand so is my hope from the **LORD**.”|Uses endurance for the disputed noun and keeps hope's named source.
3:19|Remember my affliction and wandering,\nthe wormwood and the poison.|Reads the opening as an appeal while noting possible recollection reading.
3:20|My soul remembers them again and again\nand sinks within me.|Follows the read sinking form and preserves repeated memory.
3:21|But this I bring back to mind,\nand so I have hope:|Keeps the turn dependent on remembered content rather than erasing prior suffering.
3:22|Through the **LORD**'s acts of steadfast love we have not come to an end,\nfor his compassion has not run out.|Preserves the pinned first-person plural we, with the familiar alternative noted.
3:23|They are new every morning.\nGreat is your faithfulness!|Keeps the shift to direct address and plural renewal.
3:24|“The **LORD** is my portion,” my soul says,\n“so I will hope in him.”|Retains portion as biblical vocabulary and inner speech.
3:25|The **LORD** is good to those who wait for him,\nto the person who seeks him.|Keeps waiting/seeking parallelism without changing it to passive optimism.
3:26|It is good to wait quietly\nfor the **LORD**'s salvation.|Retains salvation and quiet waiting as the poem states them.
3:27|It is good for a man\nto carry a yoke in his youth.|Preserves male noun, yoke, and life-stage image.
3:28|Let him sit alone and be silent,\nfor God has laid it on him.|Makes the implied divine agent explicit for readable pronouns; a self-assumed burden remains a noted alternative.
3:29|Let him put his mouth in the dust—\nperhaps there is hope.|Retains the tentative perhaps and extreme posture.
3:30|Let him offer his cheek to the one who strikes him;\nlet him have his fill of disgrace.|Keeps the difficult submission language in the lament's voice without turning it into advice to victims.
3:31|For the Lord will not reject forever.|Preserves the brief assertion and Lord designation.
3:32|Though he causes grief, he will show compassion\naccording to his abundant steadfast love.|Keeps grief's divine agency together with compassion.
3:33|For it is not from his heart\nthat he afflicts or grieves human beings.|Retains the heart idiom and the tension with preceding agency, explained in a note.
3:34|To crush underfoot\nall the prisoners of the earth,|Lets the infinitive list continue across labels.
3:35|to deny a man justice\nin the presence of the Most High,|Preserves justice and the divine title.
3:36|to wrong someone in a lawsuit—\ndoes the Lord not see?|Uses the rhetorical-question reading and notes the approval-reading alternative.
3:37|Who speaks and it happens\nunless the Lord has commanded it?|Keeps the rhetorical challenge to independent agency.
3:38|Do not disaster and good alike\ncome from the mouth of the Most High?|Preserves the question and both outcomes without glossing disaster as moral evil.
3:39|Why should a living man complain\nabout the consequences of his sins?|Makes the punishment sense explicit while noting the compressed sins wording.
3:40|Let us examine and search our ways\nand return to the **LORD**.|Preserves the turn to communal exhortation.
3:41|Let us lift our hearts with our hands\nto God in heaven.|Keeps inward and bodily prayer together.
3:42|We have rebelled and defied you;\nyou have not forgiven.|Preserves the unresolved accusation following confession.
3:43|You wrapped yourself in anger and pursued us;\nyou killed without pity.|Keeps the direct address and violent agency.
3:44|You wrapped yourself in a cloud\nso no prayer could pass through.|Retains the barrier-to-prayer image after the hopeful passage.
3:45|You made us refuse and filth\namong the peoples.|Preserves degrading paired nouns.
3:46|All our enemies\nopen their mouths against us.|Keeps collective hostility and the mouth image.
3:47|Terror and pit have come upon us,\ndevastation and destruction.|Preserves the fourfold compressed calamity and sound pairing.
3:48|My eye pours out streams of water\nbecause my people are shattered.|Keeps the individual voice reentering communal grief.
3:49|My eye streams without stopping,\nwithout a moment's relief,|Preserves the unfinished sentence and repeated unceasing tears.
3:50|until the **LORD** looks down\nand sees from heaven.|Keeps the conditional horizon without claiming it already happened.
3:51|What my eye sees torments my soul\nbecause of all the daughters of my city.|Retains daughters and notes the ambiguous comparative/cause expression.
3:52|Those who hated me without cause\nhunted me like a bird.|Keeps innocence claim and hunted-bird image.
3:53|They tried to end my life in a pit\nand threw stones at me.|Reads the compressed destruction in a pit with stones directed at the speaker; note gives alternative sealing stone.
3:54|Water closed over my head.\nI said, “I am cut off!”|Preserves the submerged speaker and despairing quotation.
3:55|I called your name, **LORD**,\nfrom the deepest pit.|Keeps the named appeal and depth.
3:56|You heard my voice:\n“Do not close your ear\nto my plea for relief, to my cry for help.”|Retains remembered hearing and quoted plea, noting breathing/relief sense.
3:57|You drew near when I called to you;\nyou said, “Do not fear.”|Keeps the remembered response in direct speech.
3:58|Lord, you took up the cases concerning my life;\nyou redeemed my life.|Preserves plural legal cases and redemption vocabulary.
3:59|You have seen the wrong done to me, **LORD**;\njudge my case.|Keeps divine seeing and imperative legal petition.
3:60|You have seen all their vengeance,\nall their plots against me.|Retains both hostility terms and repeated all.
3:61|You have heard their insults, **LORD**,\nall their plots against me,|Keeps hearing alongside the previous seeing and continuation into the next verse.
3:62|the words of those who rise against me,\ntheir muttering against me all day long.|Retains persistent hostile speech.
3:63|Look at them sitting and rising—\nI am their mocking song.|Preserves the whole-day posture pair and song motif.
3:64|Repay them, **LORD**,\naccording to what their hands have done.|Keeps the retributive petition as a petition.
3:65|Give them a covering over the heart;\nlet your curse be on them.|Preserves the obscure covering image and notes its possible hardening sense.
3:66|Pursue them in anger and destroy them\nfrom beneath the heavens of the **LORD**.|Retains the severe ending and third-person divine name within direct prayer.

4:1|How the gold has grown dim,
the fine gold changed!
The sacred stones lie scattered
at every street corner.|Keeps the gold and scattered sanctuary imagery without deciding all referents in the text.

4:2|Zion's precious sons,
worth their weight in pure gold—
how they are treated as clay jars,
the work of a potter's hands!|Preserves sons and the gold-to-pottery reversal.

4:3|Even jackals offer the breast
and nurse their young.
But my people have become cruel,
like ostriches in the wilderness.|Follows both read animal forms and retains the harsh poetic comparison, with cultural context in notes.

4:4|The nursing infant's tongue sticks
to the roof of its mouth from thirst.
Children ask for bread,
but no one breaks it for them.|Keeps the concrete infant suffering and bread-breaking image.

4:5|Those who ate delicacies
lie desolate in the streets.
Those raised in scarlet
embrace refuse heaps.|Preserves the class reversal and embrace image.

4:6|My people's punishment is greater
than Sodom's punishment.
Sodom was overthrown in a moment,
with no hands turned against her.|Chooses punishment sense and retains the disputed hands phrase with alternatives noted.

4:7|Her consecrated ones were purer than snow,
whiter than milk.
Their bodies were ruddier than coral,
their form like sapphire.|Keeps consecrated ones rather than deciding nobles, and preserves color/material comparisons with uncertainty noted.

4:8|Now their appearance is darker than soot;
no one recognizes them in the streets.
Their skin clings to their bones,
dry as wood.|Retains the bodily contrast without racial interpretation.

4:9|Better off are those killed by the sword
than those killed by hunger.
They waste away, pierced through
for lack of the field's produce.|Preserves the shocking comparison and hunger-as-piercing image.

4:10|The hands of compassionate women
have cooked their own children.
They became their food
when my people were shattered.|Keeps compassionate women and cannibalism together without blaming an inherent lack of care.

4:11|The **LORD** has spent his wrath,
poured out his burning anger.
He kindled a fire in Zion
that consumed her foundations.|Retains wrath exhausted and fire consuming the city's base.

4:12|The kings of the earth did not believe,
nor did anyone living in the world,
that foe and enemy could enter
Jerusalem's gates.|Preserves the sweeping claim of incredulity rather than correcting it historically.

4:13|It was because of her prophets' sins
and her priests' guilt:
they shed the blood of the righteous
within her.|Keeps leadership's specific bloodguilt and the causal fragment's relation to the fall.

4:14|They staggered blindly through the streets,\npolluted with blood,\nso that no one could touch their clothes.|Preserves blindness, pollution, and forbidden contact without changing blood to metaphor.

4:15|“Away! Unclean!” people cried at them.
“Away, away! Do not touch!”
When they fled and wandered,
people among the nations said,
“They may stay here no longer.”|Keeps repeated exclusion and displacement, marking speakers minimally.

4:17|Still our eyes failed,
watching in vain for help.
From our lookout we kept watching
for a nation that could not save.|Follows the read our form and keeps the unnamed failed ally.

4:18|They hunted our steps,
so we could not walk in our squares.
Our end drew near; our days were full.
Our end had come.|Preserves hunted movement and repeated finality.

4:19|Our pursuers were swifter
than eagles in the sky.
They chased us on the mountains
and lay in wait for us in the wilderness.|Keeps both terrains and the swift-bird comparison.

4:20|The breath of our nostrils,
the **LORD**'s anointed, was caught in their pits—
the one of whom we said,
“In his shade we will live among the nations.”|Preserves royal anointed vocabulary, breath/shade images, and the people's disappointed hope.

4:21|Rejoice and be glad, daughter Edom,
you who dwell in the land of Uz!
The cup will pass to you too;
you will become drunk and strip yourself bare.|Keeps the bitter summons, named land, and exposure without softening humiliation.
5:1|Remember, **LORD**, what has happened to us.\nLook and see our disgrace.|Keeps the communal opening petition and two seeing verbs.
5:2|Our inheritance has passed to strangers,\nour houses to foreigners.|Preserves inheritance and houses as parallel losses.
5:3|We have become orphans, fatherless;\nour mothers are like widows.|Retains the comparative like for mothers and explicit fatherlessness.
5:4|We pay silver to drink our own water;\nwe must buy our own wood.|Keeps ownership contrasted with purchase of necessities.
5:5|Our pursuers are at our necks.\nWe are exhausted and allowed no rest.|Preserves the neck image and denied relief, noting compressed syntax.
5:6|We gave our hand to Egypt,\nto Assyria, to get enough bread.|Keeps the submission gesture, both nations, and hunger motive.
5:7|Our ancestors sinned and are no more;\nwe bear their guilt.|Preserves inherited burden without explaining away the protest or harmonizing it with verse 16.
5:8|Slaves rule over us;\nno one rescues us from their hand.|Retains the social-status reversal and absent rescuer.
5:9|We risk our lives to bring in bread\nbecause of the sword in the wilderness.|Keeps danger tied to gathering food, with no invented perpetrators.
5:10|Our skin burns like an oven\nfrom hunger's scorching heat.|Preserves the heat comparison and famine's physical effect.
5:11|They raped women in Zion,\nvirgins in Judah's towns.|Makes sexual violence explicit while retaining the specific groups and locations.
5:12|Officials were hung by their hands;\nelders were shown no respect.|Keeps the bodily hanging reading and notes the alternative agency construal.
5:13|Young men carry millstones;\nboys stumble under loads of wood.|Retains forced labor and distinct age groups, with millwork alternative noted.
5:14|Elders have left the city gate;\nyoung men have stopped their music.|Keeps loss of civic life and song in parallel.
5:15|Joy has left our hearts;\nour dancing has turned to mourning.|Preserves the reversal of embodied celebration.
5:16|The crown has fallen from our head.\nWoe to us, for we have sinned!|Keeps communal confession beside earlier inherited-guilt complaint.
5:17|For this our hearts are sick;\nfor these things our eyes grow dim:|Preserves the forward-pointing explanation across labels.
5:18|Mount Zion lies desolate,\nand foxes walk over it.|Keeps the named place and animal presence without substituting a generic ruin.
5:19|But you, **LORD**, sit enthroned forever;\nyour throne endures from generation to generation.|Retains the turn to enduring kingship without making it the book's resolution.
5:20|Why do you forget us forever,\nforsake us for so many days?|Keeps the unanswered accusation and two time expressions.
5:21|Bring us back to you, **LORD**, and we will return.\nRenew our days as they were long ago—|Follows the read return form and leaves the sentence open to the last verse.
5:22|unless you have utterly rejected us\nand are angry with us beyond measure.|Preserves the unresolved conditional ending, with the stronger assertion alternative in a note.
